The following outline attempts to trace the unfolding of the letter’s thought with its mixture of planned structure and free-flowing discourse.

I. Prescript and greeting (1:1–2)

II. Blessing God who has blessed his people in Christ (1:3–14)

A. Praise to God for his grace in making believers his people (1:3–6)

B. Praise to God for his grace in redemption and revelation (1:7–10)

C. Praise to God for making his people heirs and giving them hope in Christ (1:11–12)

D. Praise to God for the conversion and future salvation of Paul’s readers (1:13–14)



III. Thanksgiving for conversion and intercession for understanding (1:15–23)

A. Thanksgiving for faith and love, and intercession for illumination (1:15–19)

B. God’s great power displayed in Christ and for the church (1:20–23)



IV. From children of wrath to new creation (2:1–10)

A. Children of wrath like all the rest (2:1–3)

B. Objects of God’s mercy (2:4–7)

C. The nature and consequences of God’s grace (2:8–10)



V. From existence without God to membership in the people of God (2:11–22)

A. The special plight of the Gentiles and God’s response (2:11–13)

B. Christ is the believing community’s peace (2:14–18)

C. Gentile Christians as an integral part of God’s household (2:19–22)



VI. Paul’s divinely given task and his suffering for the Gentiles (3:1–13)

A. Paul’s role in the administration of the mystery (3:1–7)

B. How Paul fulfills his task (3:8–13)



VII. Paul prays for his readers’ inner strength and praises the God who can give it (3:14–21)

A. Paul prays for his readers’ inner strength (3:14–19)

B. Paul praises the God who is able to strengthen his readers (3:20–21)



VIII. The growth of the church toward unity and maturity (4:1–16)

A. Christian unity and its theological basis (4:1–6)

B. The gifts of the victorious Christ cultivate the body’s maturity (4:7–16)



IX. A reminder of how to live as new human beings (4:17–5:2)

A. No longer walk as “Gentiles” but as a new human being (4:17–24)

B. Living as human beings newly created in God’s image (4:25–5:2)



X. Avoiding and transforming the deeds of darkness (5:3–14)

A. Avoiding sexual immorality and greed (5:3–7)

B. From avoidance to transformation (5:8–14)



XI. Wise conduct within the household (5:15–6:9)

A. Introduction: Wisdom and the life filled in the Spirit (5:15–20)

B. Submission in the believing household (5:21–6:9)



1. Wives and husbands (5:21–33)

2. Children and parents (6:1–4)

3. Slaves and masters (6:5–9)



XII. Standing against the strategies of the devil (6:10–20)

A. Wearing God’s protective armor (6:10–17)

B. Persevering in watchful prayer (6:18–20)



XIII. A concluding commendation and a final prayer-wish (6:21–24)

A. Tychicus and his mission (6:21–22)

B. Peace, love, faith, and grace for the letter’s recipients (6:23–24)





I. Prescript and Greeting (1:1–2)

II. Blessing God Who Has Blessed His People in Christ (1:3–14)

III. Thanksgiving for Conversion and Intercession for Understanding (1:15–23)

IV. From Children of Wrath to New Creation (2:1–10)


I. Prescript and Greeting (1:1–2)

The basic framework for the opening of Ephesians follows the conventions of Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek letters for centuries both before and after Paul’s time. Greek letters typically began with a prescript that stated the name of the sender and then the name of the recipient, often with some descriptive term added to it (“my brother,” “my sister,” “my son,” “my daughter,” “my father,” “my lord,” “esteemed,” “beloved,” or the like; Exler 1923: 23–60). After this came a word or phrase of greeting similar to the oral salutations that people gave to one another when they met in person: “Rejoice!” or “Good health!” (Lieu 1985: 163–65). Hebrew and Aramaic letters, particularly those from the first and early second century, often followed a similar pattern, with the name of the sender followed by the name of the recipient and then the common oral salutation, now changed to “Peace” (Fitzmyer 1979: 189–93; Pardee 1992: 283–84; Dion 1992: 289). In both Greek and Semitic letters, this greeting was sometimes elaborated in various ways (“Many greetings,” “Good health always,” “Peace be multiplied to you”).

At least according to the second-century literary critic Lucian, Greek philosophers sometimes changed the standard epistolary greeting to make some point consistent with their philosophical convictions. Plato replaced “Rejoice!” with “Do well!” Pythagoras and Epicurus selected “Good health!” from among the conventional options because it fit nicely with their understanding of life (Lucian, Laps. 4–6).

No known modification of the customary framework from antiquity, however, matches the creativity of Paul’s changes to it. In Ephesians, as in most of his letters, he qualifies both prescript and greeting in elaborate ways to alert his readers to the theological significance of the letter. He writes as an envoy of Christ Jesus, appointed to this office by a deliberate act of God, and he writes to God’s people in Ephesus, who believe the gospel and are in Christ. His greeting becomes not a wish for good cheer or health but a prayer similar to that of the OT priests for the grace and peace of God to rest on his readers. Paul makes clear in the greeting, however, something that he will describe more fully in the letter: that the experience of God’s grace and peace in the present, climactic period of salvation history comes to God’s people through the Lord Jesus Christ.



Exegesis and Exposition

1Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, to the saints who are ⌜in Ephesus⌝ and believers, in Christ Jesus. 2Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

[1:1] The letter begins by identifying its sender as Paul and then describing him as “an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God” (Παῦλος ἀπόστολος Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ διὰ θελήματος θεοῦ, Paulos apostolos Christou Iēsou dia thelēmatos theou). The significance we give to this identification and description will vary with the approach we take to the letter’s authorship, but it is reasonable to consider Ephesians a genuine Pauline letter, written in a later period than most of the undisputed letters and emphasizing different themes in a changed setting (see the commentary introduction).

Here Paul identifies himself as an apostle through the will of God for reasons similar to those that led him to use this same designation, or something like it, in five other letters. In Gal. 1:1; 1 Cor. 1:1; and 2 Cor. 1:1 the reason for these emphases is not far to seek: in each instance he addressed churches where people had raised questions about his apostleship (cf. Best 1997a: 32). In Rom. 1:1 and Col. 1:1 nothing clearly indicates that Paul’s apostleship was an issue, but Paul was addressing churches that he did not found and many people whom he did not know personally. He may have wanted to begin these letters, then, with a statement of the apostolic basis for the pastoral authority that he was about to exercise over his readers.

In the same way, Ephesians went to people largely unknown to Paul. He had heard only a general description of most of them (1:15; 4:21), and he could assume only that their knowledge of him was accurate (3:2). The self-description “apostle” immediately communicated why he thought he had the authority to address them in a pastoral letter.

For Paul, apostles were envoys—people whom someone or some group had sent on a specific mission. Paul could use the term of delegates that churches appointed for a special task, such as taking a gift to Paul (Phil. 2:25) or bringing monetary contributions to the needy in Jerusalem (2 Cor. 8:23). Paul could also use it in a semitechnical sense to mean someone whom God had set apart to preach the gospel (Rom. 1:1; Gal. 1:1, 15–16). In Ephesians, Paul couples apostles with prophets, and always in that order (2:20; 3:5; 4:11; cf. 1 Cor. 12:28–29; Did. 11.3). He places them at the foundation of the church (2:20) and at the head of the list of gifted people whom Christ has given to the church for its edification (4:11). For Paul, apostles played an important, authoritative role in shaping the church’s growth into what God intended the church to become (2:21; 4:13).

God had set Paul apart as a particular type of apostle. He was called to preach the gospel to non-Jewish peoples (Rom. 1:5; 11:13; Gal. 1:1, 15–16). This kind of apostleship often meant traveling with the gospel to distant places (Rom. 1:5–6, 13–14; 1 Cor. 4:9, 11; 9:5; 1 Thess. 2:1–2, 7) and frequently entailed the kind of suffering that Paul was experiencing as he wrote Ephesians (1 Cor. 4:8–15; 1 Thess. 2:1–2, 7, 9; cf. Eph. 3:1, 13; 4:1; 6:20). It also sometimes meant using letters to exercise oversight of Gentile believers whom he did not personally know (Rom. 1:5–6; 11:13; 15:15).

When Paul described himself as an apostle at the beginning of Ephesians, he probably intended to identify himself to his readers as one of the foundational guides of the church’s growth to maturity, with particular responsibility for the Gentiles in Ephesus (cf. 3:1–4, 8).

Paul identifies the recipients of his letter with the phrase τοῖς ἁγίοις τοῖς οὖσιν ἐν Ἐφέσῳ καὶ πιστοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ (tois hagiois tois ousin en Ephesō kai pistois en Christō Iēsou, to the saints who are in Ephesus and believers, in Christ Jesus). For reasons explained in the introduction to the commentary, it seems best to keep ἐν Ἐφέσῳ in the text despite its absence from the three earliest manuscripts of Ephesians and from what Basil the Great in the mid-fourth century called “the old copies” known to him. Paul wrote Ephesians about seven years after his lengthy stay in the city, and this was ample time for dramatic changes to take place among the Christian groups that flourished there. Although he was writing to a city where he had spent between two and three years, the letter has a somewhat distant tone because Paul could no longer assume that Christians he had once known in the city still lived there or were still identified with the movement, nor could he assume that all who read this letter would have a clear understanding of the important role he had played in the establishment of the church in their city (1:15; 3:2; 4:21).[1]

Does Paul address this diverse body of readers as two different groups, “the saints who are in Ephesus” and “the believers who are in Christ Jesus”? Two considerations have sometimes led interpreters to this conclusion. First, for Paul to call his readers both “saints” and “believers” seems redundant—if they are “saints,” surely they are also “believers.” Second, Paul’s repetition of the article τοῖς in front of οὖσιν ἐν Ἐφέσῳ (ousin en Ephesō, who are in Ephesus) but not in front of πιστοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ (pistois en Christō Iēsou, believers in Christ Jesus) might be understood to bind οὖσιν ἐν Ἐφέσῳ closely to ἁγίοις (hagiois, saints), which also has the article. This would leave πιστοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ to refer to a separate group. On this understanding of the Greek, Paul addresses his letter “to the saints, that is, the ones in Ephesus, and to believers who are in Christ Jesus.”

This division of the readers into two groups, however, is without precedent in Paul’s other letters, and it is difficult to see what the difference between the two groups could be. Some interpreters have suggested that Paul (or the author) wrote to Jewish Christians, whom he called “saints” (cf. 2:19; Rom. 15:25–26, 31), and Gentile Christians, whom he called “faithful” or “believers” (e.g., Kümmel 1975: 355). If this is correct, at the beginning of the letter he introduces the theme of the relationship between Gentile Christianity and ancient Israel that he will later develop at length (2:11–22). Elsewhere in the letter, however, Paul regularly calls all his readers “saints” (1:15, 18; 3:8, 18; 4:12; 5:3; 6:18), so this solution is not likely to be correct.

What, then, of the grammatical problem? Paul probably intended the first τοῖς to go both with ἁγίοις and with πιστοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ (Alford 1857: 66; Wallace 1996: 282; Hoehner 2002: 142). This is unusual, but native speakers of ancient Greek, such as Chrysostom (Hom. Eph., hom. 1; NPNF 13:51), Theodoret (R. Hill 2001: 2.33), and Theophylact (PG 124:1033) took the construction to mean that Paul was calling his readers in Ephesus both “saints” and “faithful” (or “believers”) and seemed to see nothing unnatural in it. The grammatical difficulties, then, are not insuperable, and this makes it likely that Paul addresses his readers as a single group of Christians in Ephesus who are both ἅγιοι and πιστοί.

What does he mean by these terms? The term ἅγιοι (hagioi, saints) takes its meaning from the OT, which speaks of God choosing his people from among all peoples of the earth to be “a royal priesthood and a holy [ἅγιον] nation” (Exod. 19:5–6 LXX). Because of this status, Israel should “be holy” (ἅγιοι) as God is “holy” (ἅγιος; Lev. 11:44–45; 19:2; 20:7). Israel’s holy status, given to it by God, should be lived out in holy conduct: those whom God has separated as his special people should live in a way that is separate from the surrounding environment. In Ephesians, Paul’s use of ἅγιος and related words follows the same pattern. Christ has made believers holy (ἁγιάζω, hagiazō) through the cleansing bath of the gospel (5:26), and so they have this status as a gift from God. Yet they must live in a way that is consistent with this status—they should be “holy [ἁγίους] and blameless before him in love” (1:4), and their conduct should be what is “proper for holy people [ἁγίοις]” (5:3).

The adjective πιστοί (pistoi) probably does not mean “faithful ones” in the sense of “loyal” or “trustworthy” people (e.g., Origen [Heine 2002: 81]; Lightfoot 1895: 310; Barth 1974: 67–69), although that is the most common meaning of the adjective (MM 515; BDAG 820–21). Since he will soon describe his readers as those who “have believed” (πιστεύσαντες, pisteusantes) the gospel (1:13), it is more likely that he addresses them here as “believers” in the sense that they have trusted the gospel message when they heard it (BDAG 821; Lincoln 1990: 6; O’Brien 1999: 87; Hoehner 2002: 142).

They are, moreover, both saints and believers ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ. This does not mean that they are saints who trust Christ, although that is implied, but that they are saints and believers who are “in Christ.” As the people in Ephesus whom God has set apart as his own, and who believe the gospel, they live within the sphere of existence that Christ defines.

[1:2] Paul greets his readers in exactly the same way he greets his audience in seven of his other canonical letters (Rom. 1:7b; 1 Cor. 1:3; 2 Cor. 1:2; Gal. 1:3; Phil. 1:2; 2 Thess. 1:2; Philem. 3). This greeting has linguistic similarities to the standard salutations of Greek, Hebrew, and Aramaic letters of Paul’s time, but it is also innovative and distinctive. Letters in all three languages derived their greetings from the verbal salutation that people gave to one another in social settings, χαίρειν (charein, rejoice!) in Greek and שְׁלָם/שָׁלוֹם (šālôm/šĕlām, peace!) in Hebrew/Aramaic.[2] Native Hebrew and Aramaic speakers observed the Greek norms when writing in Greek, saluting their readers not with something like εἰρήνη ὑμῖν πληθυνθείη (eirēnē hymin plēthyntheiē, may peace be increased for you) but simply with χαίρειν (cf. Lieu 1985: 166–67).[3]

Paul’s greeting seems to have its origins in a combination of both the Greek and Semitic customs. His noun χάρις (charis, grace) is semantically related to χαίρειν and sounded similar to this well-known greeting when the epistle was read aloud. Similarly, for any of his readers familiar with Jewish customs, greeting them with εἰρήνη (eirēnē, peace) probably recalled the typical Semitic salutation both in social settings and in letters. Still, Paul’s creative deviation from the conventions must have jarred those who first heard this letter (cf. Byrskog 1997: 37–38). With the term χάρις Paul was not simply saying hello, but issuing a prayer-wish that grace would come to them (cf. 6:24). Similarly, the noun εἰρήνη (eirēnē, peace) in the greeting of a Greek letter was highly unusual. Paul was not simply greeting them in Greek the way Jews said hello in Hebrew. This would have sounded as odd in ancient Greek as the greeting “Peace!” would sound in English today. Paul was instead implicitly asking God to bring peace to his readers.

Those among Paul’s readers who were familiar with Israel’s Scriptures may have recognized in Paul’s greeting the language of the priestly benediction in Num. 6:23–26.[4] Here Aaron and his sons are instructed to pray for God to “show grace” (חנַן, ḥānan; LXX: ἐλεήσαι, eleēsai) to the people of Israel and give them “peace” (שָׁלוֹם, šālôm). If Paul intended to recall this benediction, then he may have seen his distinctive greeting not only as a genuine prayer-wish for God’s people but also as an assertion of his apostolic authority (cf. Berger 1974: 199–201). Just as Jewish priests had the authority to pronounce the priestly blessing on the people, so in his role as the envoy of Christ Jesus, Paul begins his letter with a pronunciation over his readers of the blessings of grace and peace that God gives to his people.

In contrast to the priestly benediction, however, these blessings are not only from God but also from “the Lord Jesus Christ.” This anticipates the way Paul, throughout Ephesians, describes Jesus as the means by which God shows the lavishness of his grace to his people. In 1:3–6, Paul praises God for choosing his people in Christ, predestining them for adoption through Christ, and doing all this “for the praise of his glorious grace, which he graciously gave us in the Beloved.” In 2:5 it is by making believers alive together with Christ that God saves them “by grace.” In 2:7 God shows the immense riches of his grace by the kindness that he displayed in Christ Jesus. In 4:32 God shows himself to be gracious by forgiving wrongdoing in Christ (χαρίζομαι, charizomai; cf. BDAG 1078). Jesus is also the source of peace—peace between Jewish and Gentile Christians (2:14–15), between God and humankind (2:17), and together with God, among Christians generally (6:23).

Summary

Paul’s opening salutation emphasizes his authority as an apostle to instruct even Christians whom he has never seen and does not know. At least implicitly, he begins his instruction with the way he formulates the opening of this letter. He writes to those in Ephesus whom God has set apart as his people and who show this by the way they live. They believe the gospel, and their existence is defined by their relationship with Christ. As God’s people they are recipients both of God’s grace and of the peace that his grace brings, peace with God and peace with others. God the Father has given his people these blessings through the Lord Jesus Christ.



Additional Note

[1:1.] The words ἐν Ἐφέσῳ are missing in the oldest manuscript witnesses to the text of Ephesians (𝔓46, א, B). Origen (third cent.) and Basil the Great (fourth cent.) also worked with a text of Ephesians without a place name. Although Basil knew that the text was disputed at this point, he comments that the “old” copies of the letter had the reading without the place name. Still, the place name is likely to be original. Not only do the manuscripts with the name have a wider geographical distribution, but also the text without ἐν Ἐφέσῳ both violates Paul’s normal practice of including a place name at the beginning of his letters and produces almost unintelligible Greek. Probably the place name fell out of the Alexandrian manuscript tradition of the letter in an effort to further universalize its already quite general contents. For a full discussion of this important text-critical problem, see the section “The Recipients of Ephesians” in the introduction to the commentary.





I. Prescript and Greeting (1:1–2)

II. Blessing God Who Has Blessed His People in Christ (1:3–14)

III. Thanksgiving for Conversion and Intercession for Understanding (1:15–23)

IV. From Children of Wrath to New Creation (2:1–10)


II. Blessing God Who Has Blessed His People in Christ (1:3–14)

Paul often follows the greeting of his letters with a brief “prayer report” in which he describes how he thanks God for his readers in prayer (1 Thess. 1:2–3:13; 2 Thess. 1:3–12; 1 Cor. 1:4–9; Phil. 1:3–8; Rom. 1:8; Col. 1:3–8; Philem. 4–5; 2 Tim. 1:3; cf. 1 Tim. 1:12–17) and how he intercedes with God on their behalf (Phil. 1:9–11; Col. 1:9–11; Philem. 6–7; cf. Rom. 1:9–10). In 2 Cor. 1:3–4 he replaces these elements with a benediction that blesses God for his mercy and compassion in rescuing Paul from death in Asia, and allowing this experience to be the means by which he can console others in their suffering. In a way unique among his canonical letters, in Ephesians Paul not only records a thanksgiving (1:15–16) and intercessory (1:17–23) prayer report but also, before it, a lengthy benediction that blesses God for the blessings he has given to all believers, and especially to Paul’s Gentile readers.

The benediction, or berekah, has been for centuries the most common form of Jewish prayer and central to the piety of devout Jewish living. Long before the first century, Jews used both lengthy benedictions in corporate worship and brief benedictions in daily life as a way of praising God for various gracious gifts (Dahl 2000: 279–308). The benediction that David composed to celebrate the victories God had given him over his enemies (2 Sam. 22:47–49) found its way into the liturgy of ancient Israel (Ps. 18:46–48). Solomon used a benediction in a setting of corporate worship at the installation of the ark in the newly built temple (1 Kings 8:56–61). Those who returned to Israel after the Babylonian exile used a benediction in corporate worship when they gathered after the Feast of Booths to confess their sin (Neh. 9:5; cf. Pr. Azar.; Tob. 13:1–17). These benedictions sometimes do not sustain the element of praise but become intercessory prayers (1 Kings 8:57–60; Neh. 9:32; Eighteen Benedictions 4–5, 7–17), confessions of sin (Neh. 9:16–17a, 26, 28–30, 33–37; Eighteen Benedictions 6), and admonitions (1 Kings 8:61; cf. Neh. 9:38).

In everyday life, people used short benedictions as a way to express thanks to God for some good gift (1 Sam. 25:32, 39; Ezra 7:27–28; Tob. 11:14–15; Luke 1:68–75), upon receiving good news (Gen. 24:27; 1 Kings 1:48; Tob. 8:15–17; Jdt. 13:17, 18b), when giving good news (2 Sam. 18:28), to congratulate those whom God had blessed (Gen. 14:19–20; Exod. 18:10; Ruth 4:14; 1 Kings 5:7; 10:9), or simply as a greeting (1 Sam. 15:13; Tob. 11:17). They also used them to begin private, intercessory prayers (Tob. 3:11–15; 8:5–7).

The centrality of the benediction to common Jewish piety in antiquity is also clear from the Mishnah’s tractate Berakot (Benedictions), which is, significantly, the first tractate of the Mishnah’s first order. Although this tractate is difficult to date, some of its details and much of its spirit probably originated before the destruction of the temple in AD 70.[1] The tractate provides instructions for saying the regular prayers of Judaism as well as prayers over meals and occasional, spontaneous prayers.[2] The benediction (“Blessed are you, O Lord, who . . .”) is the common thread that binds all these prayers together. Some form of the Eighteen Benedictions was to be said three times a day (4.1, 3), prayers over meals took the form of benedictions (6–8), and even the morning and evening confessions of the Shema were to be preceded and concluded with benedictions (1.4). Various events in the daily routine of life were also to be greeted by blessing God: passing by a place where God had worked a miracle for Israel (9.1), seeing a display of God’s power in the natural world such as a thunderstorm (9.2), finishing construction on a house (9.3), and entering or leaving a town (9.4). Paul gives evidence in his letters of how integral such expressions of praise were to the life of a devout Jew (Rom. 1:25; 9:5; 2 Cor. 11:31).[3]

In light of all this, it is not surprising that Jewish letters sometimes opened with benedictions, or something similar to them. Three sixth-century-BC letters from Tel Arad begin with the name of the sender, a word of greeting, the name of the recipient, and then the phrase “I bless you to YHWH” (Pardee 1982: 48, 57, 64). Closer to the time of Paul, in the mid-second century BC, the Jewish historian Eupolemus retells the story of the communication between King Hiram of Tyre and Solomon (1 Kings 5:1–12; 2 Chron. 2:1–16) and, perhaps taking a hint from 2 Chron. 2:11, puts the messages between the two kings into the form of an exchange of letters (Eusebius, Praep. ev. 9.33–34; cf. Josephus, Ant. 8.50–54).[4] First Kings 5:7 says that when Hiram received a request from Solomon for Lebanese cedars to use for constructing the temple, he responded with a benediction (“Blessed be the LORD today, who has given to David a wise son to be over his great people”; 1 Kings 5:7 NRSV). Eupolemus apparently understood the retelling of this in 2 Chron. 2:11–12 to mean that Hiram (whom he calls “Souron”) put this benediction in his letter of response to Solomon.[5] In his own account, Eupolemus fashions a proper letter from “Suron” to Solomon with a prescript, greeting, and (immediately after the greeting) Hiram’s benediction. Although this evidence is too slight to be conclusive, Eupolemus’s editorial work here may mean that he was familiar with letters that followed this same form.[6] If so, then the three New Testament letters that begin with benedictions (2 Cor. 1:3–4; Eph. 1:3–14; 1 Pet. 1:3–5) may be following a Jewish epistolary custom (cf. Dahl 2000: 315–19; pace Gnilka 1971: 58n1; Lincoln 1990: 11; O’Brien 1999: 89).

Paul’s benediction in Eph. 1:3–14 is unusual because of the combination of its length, its sustained benedictory focus, and its complex series of dependent clauses. The benedictions at the beginning of other Hebrew letters are no more than a brief phrase or sentence, but Paul’s benediction, although one sentence, comprises 202 words. This makes it longer by far than the New Testament’s other epistolary benedictions: 2 Cor. 1:3–4 and 1 Pet. 1:3–5 weigh in at 44 and 53 words respectively. The longer benedictions in roughly contemporary Jewish literature and liturgy, moreover, tend to stray into intercession, confession, or admonition (cf. Caragounis 1977: 39–40, 48). They do this even when they maintain a benedictory character, as in the Eighteen Benedictions, by repeating the phrase, “Blessed are you, Lord. . . .” The benediction in Ephesians, however, sustains its praise of God from beginning to end. It announces its benedictory focus in the first line (v. 3), where the root εὐλογ- is repeated three times, once as an adjective (εὐλογητός, eulogētos, blessed), once as a participle (εὐλογήσας, eulogēsas, who has blessed), and once as a noun (εὐλογίᾳ, eulogia, blessing).[7] Although it never repeats the benedictory formula, it continues with an elaborate series of subordinate clauses that explain the blessings for which God is blessed (cf. Caragounis 1977: 40, 45) and ends with the phrase “to the praise of his glory” (v. 14; cf. vv. 6 and 12).

The Qumran literature may provide the closest parallel to the style of this benediction. Not only do its prayers often contain long sentences (Kuhn 1968: 116–17; Gnilka 1971: 56–57), sometimes punctuated with benedictions (e.g., 1QS 9.15; 1QHa 13.20; 18.14; 19.27–30), but also in 4Q434 we find a benedictory prayer that, although fragmentary, has the same broad pattern as Eph. 1:3–14. It too begins with a benedictory statement (“Bless my soul, the Lord for all his marvels, forever. And blessed be his name . . .”) and continues with a lengthy, sustained description of why God is blessed without either repeating the initial benediction or trailing off into some other kind of prayer.[8]

In the Ephesians benediction, the complex series of subordinate clauses that qualify the initial benedictory formula is so elaborate that it has produced a prodigious number of attempts to explain its structure.[9] The idea that the passage is a hymn, poem, or liturgy, perhaps one that the author took over and modified, was popular during the first half of the twentieth century (e.g., Innitzer 1904: 612–21; Lohmeyer 1926a: 120–25), although it also has more recent advocates (e.g., Coutts 1956–57: 120–24; Fischer 1973: 111–18; Lang 1969: 12–16; Muddiman 2001: 63–65).

This explanation has now fallen from favor, and for good reason. First, the style and theology of the benediction fit seamlessly into the style and theology of the rest of the letter. Stylistically, the letter contains long, complex sentences (1:3–14, 15–23; 2:1–7; 3:2–13, 14–19; 4:1–6, 11–16; 6:14–20; O’Brien 1999: 90; Hoehner 2002: 153), and theologically the rest of the letter repeats the benediction’s concern with the heavenly places, the display of God’s grace in Christ, the knowledge of God’s will, and the revelation of the mystery of God’s cosmic plans for the unity of the universe (cf. Caragounis 1977: 50–52; Pokorný 1992: 54; Best 1997a: 54–55; 1998: 109).

Second, the various attempts to uncover the poetic structure of the supposed hymn or poem by analyzing it in terms of a classical “period” that can then be divided into “cola” (Innitzer 1904: 617–18; Lohmeyer 1926a: 120–25) do not work.[10] These analyses are highly subjective (Debrunner 1926: 231), and on closer inspection, inconsistencies appear in them (van Roon 1974: 159). Attempts to improve the theological consistency or poetic symmetry of the hymn by deleting certain phrases as editorial additions do nothing to inspire confidence that this is the right approach.[11]

Attempts to organize the passage along the lines of its larger semantic structure show greater promise. The benediction has four prominent semantic features that seem to be repeated at critical junctures in the flow of its thought. First, the phrase ἐν Χριστῷ (en Christō, in Christ) or its equivalent occurs at the end of the benedictory opening (v. 3); at the end of the statement that God chose believers and predestined them to be his holy, blameless, and adoptive children (vv. 4–6); at the end of the description of Christ’s central role in the redemption of believers and in the summation of the universe (vv. 7–9); and at the end of the description of the inheritance of believers (vv. 10–12). The final paragraph does not end in the phrase but turns specifically to the readers, applying these blessings to them through the hearing of the gospel and the work of the Holy Spirit (vv. 13–14).

Second, phrases beginning with κατά (kata, according to) or the related term καθώς (kathōs, inasmuch as) and often leading to a purpose statement (vv. 4, 5b–6a, 9b–10a, 11–12, but not 7b) qualify the main clauses that describe the leading themes of the benediction. God has blessed believers (v. 3) inasmuch as (καθώς) he chose them so that they might be holy and blameless before him (v. 4). He predestined believers according to his will and for the praise of his glory (vv. 5b–6a, 11–12). God redeemed them in Christ according to the richness of his grace (v. 7). He made known to them the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure for the administration of the fullness of the times (vv. 9b–10a).

Third, the benediction has three active participles, each of which announces an important theme: εὐλογήσας (eulogēsas, who has blessed), προορίσας (proorisas, having predestined), and γνωρίσας (gnōrisas, having made known). God has blessed believers (v. 3), predestined them for adoptive sonship (v. 5), and made known to them the mystery of his cosmic purposes (v. 9).

Fourth, three times the benediction uses the refrain “for the praise of his glory” (vv. 12, 14) or “for the praise of his glorious grace” (v. 6). Each time it appears, the phrase concludes a section in which one of the three persons of the Trinity rises to special prominence: the Father (vv. 4–6), Christ (vv. 7–12), and the Holy Spirit (vv. 13–14).

Taken together, all of this shows that Paul constructed the benediction with care, but the small inconsistencies in these features also reveal the extemporaneous nature of the passage. The κατά phrases, for example, do not follow the dominant pattern consistently. The first occurrence (v. 4) uses καθώς (κατά + ὡς) rather than κατά, the third occurrence (v. 7) has no purpose clause following it, and the final occurrences feature two closely related κατά phrases with a purpose clause only after the second phrase (v. 11). Much the same is true of the three aorist active participles (εὐλογήσας, προορίσας, and γνωρίσας). Although the number of subordinate clauses that modify them show that they express leading ideas, they are not syntactically parallel with one another: εὐλογήσας is a substantival participle and is not only the chief syntactical element in verse 3 but also arguably in the entire passage. The other two participles, however, are adverbial and syntactically subordinate to their main verbs. Similarly, the phrase “for the praise of his glory” in its first occurrence appears in the expanded form “for the praise of his glorious grace” (v. 6; cf. vv. 12 and 14).

No one of these structural features, moreover, satisfactorily accounts for the whole passage. The ἐν Χριστῷ phrases (or their equivalents) come close since a good argument could be made that they stand at the end of nearly every major section (Krämer 1967: 38–41). Even so, the phrase is missing from the end of the whole passage, and instead we find εἰς ἔπαινον τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ (eis epainon tēs doxēs autou, for the praise of his glory, v. 14). If we then try to make this phrase a dominant structural marker (Innitzer 1904: 619; Coutts 1957: 116), we produce three sections of uneven length (vv. 3–6, 7–12, and 13–14). Making the three leading participles (Gnilka 1971: 59; cf. Lincoln 1990: 15–17) the dominant structural markers works no better since they can account for only verses 3–10.[12] The κατά (kata, according to) phrases (Schnackenburg 1977: 74–76; 1991: 46–47) similarly can account for only verses 3–11.

The passage therefore combines repetition of structural features and themes with small structural inconsistencies. This combination seems most likely if Paul dictated the passage extemporaneously but with some prior structure in mind before doing so.[13] It is perhaps not irrelevant that in early Christianity, and possibly in Judaism before AD 70, there is evidence that some Christians and Jews used set prayers less as statements to be repeated word for word than as outlines for directing their prayers. Although the rabbinic traditions on this are difficult to date, the Mishnah reveals that some ancient Jews used the Eighteen Benedictions as an outline for more spontaneous prayers; the variations between Matthew and Luke in the Lord’s Prayer may also be a result of this practice.[14] If Paul used this method in 1:3–14, then he may have had some set form of prayer in mind, either a prayer form that he created when he planned the composition of the letter or a traditional form that others also knew.

Our best chance for recovering the basic structure of Paul’s prayer seems to lie in observing where the dominant structural patterns converge and in observing the thematic emphases in the sections that result. The two features that converge most consistently seem to be the ἐν (en, in) phrases that refer to Christ (Krämer 1967) and the κατά (kata, according to) phrases that refer to the manner in which God has blessed believers in Christ and the purpose for which he has done so (Schnackenburg 1977: 74–75; 1991: 46–47). Using these two features, we can divide the benediction into four major parts. The beginning and end of the passage express praise to God, and the internal boundaries of each part are marked by an ἐν phrase referring to Christ at the end of a section followed by ἐν ᾧ (en hō, in whom) at the beginning of the next section.[15] Thus the first section begins with the benedictory formula (v. 3) and ends with ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ (en tō ēgapēmenō, in the Beloved, v. 6). The second section begins with ἐν ᾧ (v. 7) and ends with ἐν αὐτῷ (en autō, in him, v. 10). The third section begins with ἐν ᾧ (v. 11) and ends with ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ (v. 12). The final section begins with ἐν ᾧ (v. 13) and ends with an expression of praise (v. 14).

Embedded in the first three of the sections that these three internal boundary markers demarcate is a κατά clause followed by a purpose clause. The final section has no such construction and has two ἐν ᾧ clauses, indicating that its function is different from the other three. This difference receives confirmation in the switch from the first person, which dominates the first three sections (vv. 3–12), to the second person in this final section (vv. 13–14).

A diagram of the structure looks like this:

Section Introduction Conclusion Κατά Phrase + Purpose Clause

A. 1:3–6

Opening expression of praise: εὐλογητὸς ὁ θεός (eulogētos ho theos, blessed is the God) ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ (en tō ēgapēmenō, in the Beloved) κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν . . . εἰς ἔπαινον δόξης τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ (kata tēn eudokian . . . eis epainon doxēs tēs charitos autou, according to the good pleasure . . . for the praise of his glorious grace)

B. 1:7–10

ἐν ᾧ ἔχομεν (en hō echomen, in whom we have) ἐν αὐτῷ (en autō, in him) κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν . . . εἰς οἰκονομίαν (kata tēn eudokian . . . eis oikonomian, according to the good pleasure . . . for administering)

C. 1:11–12

ἐν ᾧ καὶ ἐκληρώθημεν (en hō kai eklērōthēmen, in whom also we have been made heirs) ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ (en tō Christō, in Christ) κατὰ τὴν βουλὴν . . . εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἡμᾶς εἰς ἔπαινον δόξης αὐτοῦ (kata tēn boulēn . . . eis to einai hēmas eis epainon doxēs autou, according to the counsel . . . that we might exist for the praise of his glory)

D. 1:13–14

ἐν ᾧ καὶ ὑμεῖς ἀκούσαντες . . . ἐν ᾧ καὶ πιστεύσαντες (en hō kai hymeis akousantes . . . en hō kai pisteusantes, in whom also you, when you heard . . . in whom also, when you believed) Closing expression of praise: εἰς ἔπαινον τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ (eis epainon tēs doxēs autou, for the praise of his glory) [none]

If we now allow this structure to inform the outline of the ideas expressed in the passage, we discover a threefold development followed by a specific application. In the first section (A) Paul praises God for everything he has done for his people in Christ and then describes the first of these blessings. God chose his people in Christ before creation to be his adopted children. He did this in accordance with the good pleasure of his will and as a praiseworthy display of his glorious grace (vv. 3–6). In the second section (B) Paul describes how God showed the richness of his grace to his people in two ways, first by redeeming them through Christ’s sacrificial death and then by making known to them his purpose for the unification of everything in the universe in Christ (vv. 7–10). In the third section (C) Paul summarizes the first two sections by describing again how God made his people heirs (recalling the motif of adoptive sonship from section 1) in accord with his will (recalling the emphasis on his will in sections 1 and 2) and so that they might praise his glory (recalling the emphasis on his praiseworthy and glorious grace in sections 1 and 2; vv. 11–12). In the fourth section (D), Paul turns directly to his readers to remind them that when they heard and believed the gospel, God sealed them with his Spirit, preserving them for future salvation and providing a down payment on their future inheritance (vv. 13–14). All this, Paul says in the passage’s last phrase, has happened for the praise of God’s glory (v. 14). The passage therefore ends as it began, with an expression of praise to God.

The passage has a trinitarian character, as many interpreters have properly noticed (e.g., Innitzer 1904: 614; Lohmeyer 1926a: 122; O’Brien 1999: 91; Hoehner 2002: 64, 159), but its main focus is Christ (cf. Fee 1994: 665). The ten “in” statements referring to Christ, six of them forming the hinges on which the structure of the passage swings, give it an unmistakably christological emphasis. Other elements of the passage also revolve around Christ: the benedictory opening (v. 3), doxological conclusion (vv. 13–14; cf. vv. 6, 12), and explanatory κατά phrases (vv. 5b–6, 7b, 9b–10, 11b–12) all are designed to praise God for his gracious redemption of believers in Christ.[16]

The practical purpose for including such a benedictory prayer in this letter becomes clear at its conclusion, where Paul turns specifically to all who read it or hear it read and, on the basis of what God has done for them, draws them into his expression of praise. If we can take 3:13 to mean that Paul’s readers were discouraged, Paul may have written this benediction to remind them of all that God has done for them in Christ and of the important place that they, as the church, occupy in God’s historical purposes.
